_summary:
Four of the seven hard cases have been run on real photos: plaid shirt, graphic tee, white sneakers and jeans, plus a textured knit as an extra. Striped sweater, floral and camouflage are not tested yet because the photo source rate-limited the build environment.

Styles A, B and C draw the same parametric shape in three looks. Style D traces the photo's outline and is shown only to explain why it was rejected. Pick between A, B and C. Updated: shirt collars are redrawn, seams and buttons now stay visible on patterned cloth, and patterns follow the sleeves.

Nothing here has been through the app's real tagging call yet; the attributes were set by hand.

plaid-flannel.verdict: Works: the real plaid tiles cleanly inside the drawn shirt
points: The repeat was found automatically and one repeat is used as the tile, so the scale is close to the photo's.
Collar, buttons, curved hem and low pockets come from the attributes, not the photo.
After feedback: the collar was redrawn as a proper point collar, seams are now drawn dark over a pale halo so they show on the pattern, and the plaid turns to follow the sleeves and collar.
The cutout kept the dress form's neck and base; a hung or flat photo would not have that problem.
Style D (traced) shows why tracing the photo was rejected: the outline depends on how the item happened to hang.

plaid-madras.verdict: Partly: reads as a blue madras, but duller than the shirt and missing its yellow and green bands
points: The photo is only 600px and shot at an angle, so the cleanest patch of cloth is small and from the shaded side.
No reliable repeat was found, so the tile is mirrored; the mirroring leaves faint symmetrical marks.
Expect better from a straight-on phone photo. This is the case to re-check with real photos.

marl-sweater.verdict: Works: the knit texture carries over and the shape is right
points: The turtleneck needed a new neck option, which took a few lines. Expect the shape vocabulary to grow like this as real items show up.
A plain colour would also have been acceptable here; the texture tile is a bonus.

graphic-tee.verdict: Works: the real print is lifted off the photo and placed on the drawing
points: The print keeps its position and size relative to the shirt. Nothing is redrawn, so the text stays legible.
The photo's warm light made the shirt measure pink-cream; the attribute word 'white' pulls it back. Without that word it would be drawn cream.
A soft shadow by the sleeve was first mistaken for part of the print; prints are now told from shadows by their crisp edges.

jeans.verdict: Works: right shape and a believable denim blue
points: The colour is the lit part of the denim, not the average including creases.
Fading and whiskering are not shown. That is deliberate for a flat illustration; the real photo is one tap away.

sneakers-pair.verdict: Partly: clearly a white low sneaker, but a generic one
points: Measured from the photo alone the shoes came out mid-grey because most of the surface is in shadow. The attribute word 'white' corrects it.
The drawing is a single side-on shoe whatever the photo's angle, so a pair shot at three-quarters is not a problem.
Model-specific details (the black toe stripe here) are not shown. Shoes are the weakest template and need the most work.

sneaker-held.verdict: Partly: white low sneaker with a thick sole, but the orange side logo is lost
points: Prints on shoes are not carried over yet; the photo's angle does not match the side-on drawing.
The cutout left a faint ghost of the hand. It does not affect the drawing, but the stored cutout would look odd.
